description:
I am a Mechanical Engineer with a strong interest in Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Data Analytics, and Fire Safety Engineering. My background includes mechanical engineering, 3D modelling, data analysis, and exploring AI-driven solutions for real-world engineering challenges.

I am currently developing FLARE-X – Flame Learning and Analysis for Risk Evaluation, a research project focused on understanding flame behaviour under microgravity conditions using combustion data.
summary:
We developed FLARE-X (FLEX Fire Safety Insights · PSI-69), an interactive, AI-powered aerospace fire-safety analytics platform created for the NASA Space Apps Flame in Freefall challenge. The platform transforms raw microgravity combustion telemetry from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository—specifically the International Space Station’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (FLEX, PSI-69) alongside multi-facility orbital combustion investigations—into real-time predictive insights using a browser-native Random Forest and Physics-Informed Ridge machine learning engine, interactive 3D/4D visualizations, and habitat gap simulators.

In space, the absence of gravity eliminates natural buoyant convection, causing flames to burn spherically, persist at lower oxygen levels, and transition into stealth, low-temperature "cool flames" that evade standard smoke and optical detectors. FLARE-X directly addresses this challenge by predicting droplet extinction diameters and burn rates, mapping unverified atmospheric regimes (such as oxygen-enriched lunar habitats and EVA suits), and ranking fire-safety engineering priorities across spacecraft environments.

This work is vital because Earth-based fire codes fail in microgravity and partial gravity. By translating complex orbital flight data into actionable detection, ventilation, and suppression guidance, FLARE-X helps protect astronauts on future Artemis lunar bases, Mars missions, and commercial stations.
details:
1. What It Does & How It Works

FLARE-X (FLEX Fire Safety Insights · PSI-69) transforms raw microgravity combustion telemetry from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository—specifically 274 experimental runs from the International Space Station’s Flame Extinguishment Experiment (PSI-69 FLEX) alongside multi-facility orbital combustion records—into real-time predictive fire-safety intelligence.

  • Browser-Native Machine Learning Pipeline: A custom client-side ML engine trains a Random Forest Classifier (bootstrap CART decision trees) and a Hybrid Random Forest + Physics-Informed Ridge Regressor directly in the browser across all 274 ISS flight runs, validated by a distance-weighted k-NN (k = 7) consensus check. It predicts droplet flame outcomes (Radiative Extinction, Complete Burnout, or Droplet Disruption), burning rate constant (K), flame extinction diameter (dext), and a Cool-Flame Reignition Index.
  • Interactive Telemetry & Physics Simulation: Across 10 specialized mission modules, users filter runs by fuel (heptane vs. methanol), chemical suppressant (CO2, He, or none), and chamber pressure (0.7–3.1 atm); inspect a clickable 2D Random Forest Decision Surface Phase Map; evaluate atmospheric coverage gaps for Moon and Mars habitats; and run an animated d2-law droplet simulator visualizing the transition from a bright hot flame (2,200–3,100 °F) to a stealth low-temperature "cool flame" (400–1,000 °F).

2. Benefits & Intended Impact

On Earth, gravity drives buoyant convection that pulls fresh oxygen into a flame and carries hot gases upward. In microgravity, molecular diffusion is ~100× slower, causing flames to burn spherically at lower oxygen thresholds and linger as invisible cool flames that evade conventional optical and smoke sensors.

  • Deep-Space Crew Protection: Provides mission planners with habitat-specific safety rankings (ISS, Lunar Base, Mars Habitat, Pressurized Rover) and flags unverified atmospheric regimes—such as low-pressure, oxygen-enriched Artemis habitats (≤ 0.69 atm, ≥ 30% O2) and EVA spacesuits (100% O2 at 0.29 atm) ahead of upcoming LUCI and FM2 flights.
  • Terrestrial Engineering Spin-Offs: Translates orbital extinguishment and cool-flame kinetics into cleaner Halon-replacement fire suppressants (fine water mist and inert gas blends), multi-spectrum early-warning smoke detectors, low-emission internal combustion engines, and confined-space fire safety for submarines and high-altitude aircraft.

Authoritative Data Sources

NASA PSI-69 (FLEX), NASA/TP-2015-216046, CIR / MSG / Cygnus / WSTF

Supplies verified orbital droplet combustion telemetry, hardware metadata, and Limiting Oxygen Index benchmarks.

4. Creativity & Key Design Factors Considered

  • Zero-Dependency, Instant-Load Execution: To guarantee rock-solid reliability in offline or firewalled demo and mission-control environments, the dashboard executes its entire Random Forest and Ridge training pipeline, chart rendering, and physics simulations client-side in under 15 ms with zero external CDN dependencies.
  • Explainable AI & Plain-English Accessibility: Pairs rigorous thermodynamic metrics (pO2, d2-law decay, confusion matrices, and local feature attributions) with a dedicated Judge Pitch Guide translating microgravity combustion physics into clear everyday analogies.
  • Strict Scientific Guardrails: Separates low-velocity crew-cabin fire physics (0–30 cm/s) from rocket propellant combustion (LH2/LOX thrust chambers), transparently labels analyst rubric weights, flags out-of-distribution extrapolations, and enforces NASA-STD-3001 non-autonomic decision-support boundaries.

Core Takeaway: Terrestrial fire codes fail when gravity disappears. By uniting 274 verified ISS combustion experiments with explainable client-side machine learning, physical sensor telemetry, and interactive habitat gap analysis, FLARE-X equips aerospace engineers to detect and prevent invisible fires before they threaten a crew.
